spec.title: A tested validator under change control
spec.intro:
You own the laptop-encryption control. A directory of raw evidence records — one JSON
file per laptop, plus the inevitable malformed one — needs a tool that judges each
record, survives the bad file, and lives in a Git repository whose history is itself
change-management evidence. The Git on this box is real: every commit, branch, and
merge below is genuine repository state, and the checks verify that state — not the
text on your screen. One honest boundary: this box does not execute Python. You will
author the validator and its tests here as real, runnable code (the checks read what
you wrote), and the module's §6 lab on your own machine is where pytest actually runs
it. The pull-request review step has no command-line form anywhere; you will take the
solo path §6 allows — self-review, noted — and the merge records the reviewed change.

tasks.instruction:
Orient, then provision. Find the lab directory and enter it, generate the evidence
fixtures with the lab's own script — `bash labs/setup.sh evidence/` — list what it
wrote, and read the one file that is going to cause all the trouble:
`evidence/lt-05.json`. Look at it closely. What will a JSON parser do with that?

hints.nudge: `ls` from home shows the lab directory. The setup script is inside it, under `labs/` — and it takes the destination directory as its argument.

hints.concept: §6 Setup — the lab generates its own fixtures so every learner judges identical evidence

hints.reveal: cd lab05, then: bash labs/setup.sh evidence/ · ls evidence · cat evidence/lt-05.json

tasks.explain:
Five records, one per laptop — and lt-05.json is truncated mid-value: not valid
JSON, exactly the kind of input a real collector emits when something dies halfway.
The script's output here is the real thing: the simulator replays the same bytes a
real Linux box produces running the same committed script.

tasks.instruction:
Make the directory a repository and put a clean starting point on `main`: run
`git init`, create an empty `validator.py` (`touch` does it), stage it, and commit
it with a message that says what this commit is. From here on, every change to the
control's logic is on the record.

hints.nudge: Four moves: initialise, create the empty file, stage it, commit it. The commit needs `-m "a message"` — there is no editor hand-off in this lab.

hints.concept: §4.7 — a commit is who/what/when/why, hash-bound and tamper-evident

hints.reveal: git init · touch validator.py · git add validator.py · git commit -m "Start with an empty validator on main"

tasks.explain:
That commit is real repository state — the checker read the repo's object store,
not your screen. An empty first commit sounds trivial, but it pins the moment the
control's logic came under change management: everything after this has an author,
a timestamp, and a reason.

tasks.instruction:
Write the control's atom. In `validator.py`, define `evaluate(record)`: return
`"PASS"` when `record["encrypted"]` is exactly `True`, else `"FAIL"` — a record
*missing* the field must FAIL, and so must `"encrypted": "yes"`. Then write three
tests in `test_validator.py` — good record passes, unencrypted fails, missing
field fails — and commit both files on `main`. (The editor or a heredoc both work;
this is real code your own machine's pytest must accept in §6.)

hints.nudge: Truthiness is the trap: `record.get("encrypted")` treats the string "yes" as true and a missing field as false-by-accident. The module's form compares against `True` itself.

hints.concept: §4.4 + §4.6 — a judgment in a function is testable; absence of evidence is not evidence of compliance

hints.reveal: In validator.py: def evaluate(record): return "PASS" if record.get("encrypted") is True else "FAIL" — in test_validator.py, three tests asserting evaluate({"host": "lt-01", "encrypted": True}) == "PASS", evaluate({"host": "lt-02", "encrypted": False}) == "FAIL", evaluate({"host": "lt-03"}) == "FAIL" — then git add both files and git commit

tasks.explain:
The `is True` comparison encodes a GRC judgment, not a style preference: missing
evidence is not compliance, and neither is a string that merely looks affirmative.
The third test is the one beginners skip — it pins the policy that absence fails.
These checks read your code's shape; proving its behavior is what running the
suite in §6 is for.

tasks.instruction:
Scale the judgment. Add `validate_dir(path)` to `validator.py`: loop over every
file in the directory, parse each as JSON, call `evaluate`, collect
`{file, verdict}` results. Reality check: when this loop hits `lt-05.json`,
`json.loads` raises and — unprotected — the whole run dies at file 5 of 5. Wrap
the parse in `try`/`except` so a malformed file becomes a recorded
`{file, error}` entry and the loop continues to judge the good files.

hints.nudge: The risky line is the parse. Put only that in the `try:`; in the `except`, append `{"file": name, "error": str(e)}` to an errors list and `continue` the loop.

hints.concept: §4.5 — an evidence collector that dies on row 3 of 500 silently loses 497 records

hints.reveal: def validate_dir(path): results, errors = [], [] — for name in sorted(os.listdir(path)): try: with open(os.path.join(path, name)) as f: record = json.loads(f.read()) — except (OSError, ValueError) as e: errors.append({"file": name, "error": str(e)}); continue — else append {"file": name, "verdict": evaluate(record)} to results; return {"results": results, "errors": errors}

tasks.explain:
Data + decisions + repetition: a loop, a parse, a judgment — and the parse wrapped
so one bad file becomes a finding instead of a crash. That `except` clause is the
difference between a brittle script and a defensible evidence tool: the report
will say *exactly* which inputs could not be judged, and why.

tasks.instruction:
Prove the graceful handling — with a test that asserts real behavior. Add
`test_malformed_is_recorded...` to `test_validator.py`: run `validate_dir` over
`evidence/` and assert BOTH that the malformed file landed in `errors` AND that
good files still received verdicts in `results`. A test that merely calls the
function and asserts nothing is coverage padding, and it is forbidden.

hints.nudge: Two asserts, two behaviors: one reaches into the report's errors list for lt-05.json, one checks a known-good verdict is still present in results.

hints.concept: §4.6 — every assertion checks an observable outcome that maps to real behavior

hints.reveal: def test_malformed_is_recorded_and_good_files_still_judged(): report = validate_dir("evidence") — assert any(e["file"] == "lt-05.json" for e in report["errors"]) — assert {"file": "lt-01.json", "verdict": "PASS"} in report["results"]

tasks.explain:
This is the assertion that proves the control's resilience — not a line touched
for a coverage number. If someone later "simplifies" the try/except away, this
test goes red; if an error starts swallowing good files, this test goes red. The
checker verified both asserts exist and touch both lists.

tasks.instruction:
Make the tool emit its EVIDENCE artifact: add report-writing to `validator.py` so
a run writes `report.json` containing both `results` and `errors` — what was
judged, and what honestly could not be. Use `json.dumps` and write the file; the
report a non-programmer opens next quarter must carry both lists.

hints.nudge: One small function: take the dict validate_dir returns, json.dumps it, write it to report.json with open(..., "w").

hints.concept: §5.2 — an honest report shows the verdicts AND the list of what couldn't be evaluated

hints.reveal: def write_report(path, out="report.json"): report = validate_dir(path) — with open(out, "w") as f: f.write(json.dumps(report, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + "\n") — return report

tasks.explain:
The judgment stopped being something a human does by eye and became an artifact a
machine writes the same way every time. An auditor reading report.json sees four
verdicts and one recorded error — the unevaluable file is *in* the evidence, not
silently missing from it.

tasks.instruction:
Your malformed-handling work (tasks 4–6) is sitting uncommitted — exactly the
state change management exists for. Deliver it as a reviewed feature: cut the
branch `git switch -c handle-malformed` (your edits ride along), stage and commit
both files there with a message that explains WHY, self-review the change (the
solo path §6 allows — read your own diff and note it in the message or your
head), then `git switch main` and `git merge handle-malformed`.

hints.nudge: Branch = isolation, commit message = the why field of the change record, merge = the approved change joining the main line. Five commands in all.

hints.concept: §4.7 — branch → commit → review → merge IS the change-management control, generated as a by-product of working correctly

hints.reveal: git switch -c handle-malformed · git add validator.py test_validator.py · git commit -m "Record malformed evidence files as errors instead of crashing" · git switch main · git merge handle-malformed

tasks.explain:
The repository state the checker just verified — feature branch exists, main's
tip carries the malformed-handling change, history has the full chain — is the
change-management evidence itself. Nobody "collected" it. On a shared remote the
review happens on a pull request before the merge; the control elements are the
same ones you just produced locally.

tasks.instruction:
Read your own audit trail: run `git log --oneline --graph` and read it bottom-up
as a change-management record — the clean starting point, the encryption check
arriving on main, the malformed-handling change isolated and then joining the
main line. Which commit would you show an auditor who asks "who changed the
control's logic, and why"?

hints.nudge: It's one command — the same one §5.3 reads aloud. The graph drawing comes from the real commit DAG you built.

hints.concept: §5.3 — the log IS the evidence: re-runnable, tamper-evident, attributable

tasks.explain:
Those hashes are real content-addressed commit ids from the repository you built —
alter any commit and every hash after it changes, which is why this record is
tamper-evident. Your history reads linearly because the merge was a fast-forward;
on a shared remote with a pull request, the same flow grows the §5.3 merge bubble.

tasks.instruction:
Two judgments, three or four sentences each, written for a non-programmer
colleague. First: why is "missing field → FAIL" the GRC-correct choice — what
would the control silently become if absence passed? Second: §5.4's two kinds of
red — when this tool runs for real, how do you tell "my logic is wrong" (a
failing assertion in pytest) from "the input was malformed and the program
correctly said so" (an entry in report.json's errors), and why does confusing
them either ship a broken control or chase ghosts?

hints.nudge: Start from what the evidence CAN'T show: a record with no encrypted field proves nothing — and a control that treats 'nothing' as 'pass' is no longer measuring encryption.

hints.concept: §5.4 — a failing assertion means fix the code; a recorded error means the code worked and the input was bad

tasks.instruction:
Map each Git step you performed onto the change-management control element it
satisfies, in your own words (two or three sentences): the branch, the
explain-why commit, the review (here: your noted self-review; on a team: a pull
request approved by someone who is not the author), and the merge. Then say what
a program is — data + decisions + repetition — and where each of the three lives
in the validator you just built.

hints.nudge: Branch = the change can't touch the main line until approved. Commit message = the why field. Review = segregation of duties. Merge = the approved change, recorded forever.

hints.concept: §3 — Git is not LIKE a change-management control; for your code, it IS one

files.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Module 05 lab fixture generator (original lab asset).
# Usage: setup.sh [DEST_DIR]   (default ./evidence)
# Produces a directory of laptop encryption-status evidence records (one JSON per host),
# including: a passing host, a failing host, a host MISSING the encrypted field,
# and one deliberately MALFORMED file (not valid JSON) to exercise graceful handling.
set -euo pipefail
DEST="${1:-./evidence}"
mkdir -p "$DEST"

cat > "$DEST/lt-01.json" <<'JSON'
{"host": "lt-01", "encrypted": true, "checked_at": "2026-05-28"}
JSON

cat > "$DEST/lt-02.json" <<'JSON'
{"host": "lt-02", "encrypted": false, "checked_at": "2026-05-28"}
JSON

# Host with the field absent entirely — absence must NOT count as a pass.
cat > "$DEST/lt-03.json" <<'JSON'
{"host": "lt-03", "checked_at": "2026-05-28"}
JSON

cat > "$DEST/lt-04.json" <<'JSON'
{"host": "lt-04", "encrypted": true, "checked_at": "2026-05-28"}
JSON

# Deliberately malformed: truncated, not valid JSON. The validator must record this
# as an error and keep going, NOT crash the whole run.
cat > "$DEST/lt-05.json" <<'JSON'
{"host": "lt-05", "encrypted": tr
JSON

echo "Module 05 fixtures written to $DEST (5 files: 2 pass, 1 fail, 1 missing-field, 1 malformed)"
